About the show

A small show.
On purpose.

Slow Burn Stories is an independent interview podcast about the people quietly building things that matter. There is no parent network, no advertiser to keep happy, and no algorithm I'm trying to please. Just the conversation, the microphone, and the time.

The origin

Why this exists.

I spent the better part of eight years editing a regional culture magazine in San Francisco. The work was good and the people were kind, but every story we shipped felt a little compressed — flattened into 1,200 words and three pull quotes when it deserved 6,000 and three hours.

In 2021 a profile I'd commissioned of a small-batch knifemaker came in at 11,000 words. It was the best thing the writer had ever turned in. We cut it to 1,400. The knifemaker, when I called to apologize, was gracious about it. The writer was not. Neither was I, honestly. I think that was the moment.

The following spring I bought a Shure SM7B on a payment plan, asked my then-partner to help me hang acoustic panels in the garage, and started cold-emailing people whose work I admired. The deal: an hour minimum, no PR person on the line, no questions sent in advance, no clock. Just a conversation that gets to find its own shape.

I've now made sixty-four of these. The deal has held.

The thing about an hour is that you can't fake it. Around minute thirty-eight the small talk runs out and the actual conversation begins.

That's the whole show, really. The first half is preparation. The second half is what we came for.

Cassia · at the desk
The host

Cassia Romero.

Editor turned host · Oakland, CA

Cassia grew up in Albuquerque, the youngest of three. Her parents ran a small print shop downtown until 2014. She likes to think the show is, in some quiet way, descended from the long Saturday-afternoon conversations her father used to have with the people who came in to pick up wedding invitations.

After college she worked at three different print magazines — first as a fact-checker, then a writer, then features editor — before her last masthead title at Pacific Quarterly. She left in early 2022 to start the show full-time. She lives in a small house in the Dimond district with a 14-year-old cattle dog named Murph and a constantly rotating cast of houseplants she insists she does not have time to care for.

She has been to journalism school exactly zero times. She thinks this has mostly been an asset.

cassia [at] slowburnstories.fm · @cassiaromero · Oakland

How it's made

A garage, two microphones,
and a lot of patience.

There is no studio team, no remote engineer, no green room. Most weeks it's just me, the guest, two SM7Bs, and a kettle. Here's how an episode actually gets made — from first email to release.

01 · Six to eight weeks before

Research.

Every guest starts with a deep read. I block off three to four full days. I read everything they've published or that's been written about them — books, papers, old podcast appearances, court filings if relevant. I make a long single-document timeline. I rarely use more than 10% of it. That's the point.

02 · The week of

Record.

Most guests come to Oakland — the garage has a couch, a Persian rug, decent coffee, and remarkably little sound bouncing around. Remote guests record locally on a kit I ship them two weeks ahead. We do a 20-minute warm-up that's not recorded, then we go.

03 · The week after

Edit.

I edit every episode myself. Three full days in Reaper, usually starting Wednesday. My sound designer Eitan does the final mix on Sunday — leveling, light noise reduction, the gentle bed of room tone we use under the cold opens. Master goes out Monday night.

The setup.

For the gear-curious. None of this matters as much as the conversation, but the questions come in often enough that I figured I'd list it.

Item What I use Notes
Microphones Shure SM7B (×2) Cloudlifter CL-1 inline boost on each
Interface Focusrite Scarlett 4i4 Gen 3. Quiet enough for vocal podcast work.
Headphones Sony MDR-7506 The cheap classics. Two pairs. One guest, one me.
Treatment GIK 244 bass traps · DIY rockwool panels Garage door insulated with mineral wool sandwich.
Editing Reaper · iZotope RX 10 standard Mouth declick is the only RX module I really lean on.
Remote guest kit Samson Q2U + foam screen + USB Shipped two weeks ahead, returned post-paid.
Hosting Transistor.fm No prefix trackers. Direct RSS, same since ep one.
The credits

The (very small) team.

Two people, both part-time. Both essential.

Eitan Cohen-Mizrahi Sound design & final mix

Eitan has mixed every episode since the first one. He is a film composer by training — the gentle, almost-not-there beds you hear under the cold opens and the credits are entirely his. He works out of his apartment in Echo Park.

Priya Anand-Kowalski Editorial researcher · show notes

Priya joined the show in late Season 2. She handles fact-checking, link gathering, and the dense little timestamped show notes you'll find on every episode page. She is a former librarian. It shows.

The garage itself Recording space · co-founder

Detached, single car, behind a Craftsman in the Dimond district. It was a shed when I moved in. It has a couch, a rug, a kettle, and (most importantly) no compressor humming on the other side of the wall. It deserves a credit.

In the wild

What listeners and editors have said.

Honestly the show doesn't get covered all that often. These are some of the kinder things people have written. The "Best Podcasts of 2024" nod from The Audio Quarterly was an enormous and slightly bewildering surprise.

"The patience Romero brings to her interviews is the kind that gets quieter the longer it lasts. Around the forty-five-minute mark her guests stop performing and just talk. It is the rarest thing in audio right now."
— The Audio Quarterly · Best of 2024
"Slow Burn Stories is what magazine profile journalism would sound like if it had three hours and a microphone instead of three thousand words and a deadline."
— Longform Newsletter · Recommended
"I drive a forklift. I listened to the episode with the apiarist twice. The second time I cried at a stoplight. Thank you."
— listener email · February 2025
"The kind of independent podcast that makes the case, almost by accident, for what an independent podcast can still be."
— Hot Pod News · Indie Spotlight
